Comparing 15 Spec-Driven Development Frameworks, Artifacts, and Decision Paths— SDD

Jarosław Wasowski

From Spec-Kit at ~90k stars to MUSUBI at 28 — a full ecosystem map with an 8-dimensional matrix and decision paths per context.

Spec-Driven Development Frameworks in the AI Coding Era

Superpowers has 166,000 stars on GitHub — the most in the Spec-Driven Development category. MUSUBI has 28. Both solve the same problem — disciplining an AI agent through specification — and they do it in radically different ways. Superpowers installs with a single command and gives you a HARD-GATE in prompts. MUSUBI requires nine articles of a constitution, the EARS format, a traceability matrix, and C4 diagrams.

Both are rational choices. Let me show you why.

In this article, I break down fifteen SDD frameworks, show exactly what they install, and map them onto Piskala’s 2026 three-level rigor taxonomy. The goal: in ten minutes you know which one fits your project — and why not the other way around.

What You’ll Learn

  • A map of 15 frameworks in one table — from Superpowers’ 166k stars to MUSUBI’s 28, from enterprise Intent ($252M in funding) to academic CSDD, all ordered by rigor level, not popularity.
  • Three rigor levels as a contract map — Spec-First (letter of intent), Spec-Anchored (BIM with addendums), Spec-as-Source (CNC model) as a tool-selection compass.
  • What .specify/ actually contains — nine articles of Spec-Kit's constitution from Library-First Principle to Integration Over Isolation, plus spec/plan/tasks templates.
  • Superpowers — the 166k-star plugin with ironclad TDD — how HARD-GATE works, which skill files it installs, wave-based execution with subagents.
  • MUSUBI with EARS, C4, ADR, and a traceability matrix — five EARS patterns, nine constitutional articles, 100% REQ→Design→Code→Test coverage.
  • .spec.md with @generate, Tessl Spec Registry, CSDD — what literally goes into the file, how // GENERATED FROM SPEC - DO NOT EDIT works, how CSDD reduces security defects by 73%.
  • A matrix of 15 tools and four decision paths — solo, enterprise, brownfield, security-critical with concrete recommendations and startup commands.
  • Horizon 2026+ — MCP as universal protocol, AGENTS.md as a cross-tool standard, Living Spec as infrastructure.

Have a look at this piece I wrote too: SDD Writing Specifications for AI: BDD as the Missing Link — Spec-Driven Development

Fifteen Answers to One Problem

The Spec-Driven Development ecosystem in 2026 comprises fifteen actively developed frameworks covering the full spectrum — from zero-config plugin (Superpowers) to academic methodology (CSDD). Most analyses I see in industry reviews focus on two or three of the most popular tools. That’s a systemic error. Only the full panorama reveals the real market structure — and it doesn’t map onto star popularity.

The big picture in numbers looks like this (as of April 2026). On the OSS side, Superpowers (166k stars) and Spec-Kit (~90k stars) lead. Behind them: BMAD-METHOD (~45k stars), GSD (~48k stars), OpenSpec (5.8k stars), cc-sdd (1.5k stars). Further down: SpecSwarm (57 stars), OWASP Security Skill (145 stars), and MUSUBI with its 28 stars closing the publicly countable field.

Beyond the GitHub count, five significant players operate: Don Cheli SDD (93+ commands, code-level TDD gate), Agent OS v3 (enhancer), Shotgun CLI (generator), WordPress SDD Constitution (domain-specific), and CSDD as an academic methodology (arXiv:2602.02584).

The commercial segment includes Intent from Augment Code ($252 million in funding, bidirectional Living Spec) and Tessl by Guy Podjarny ($125 million, the only framework aspiring to Spec-as-Source in production). Together with open-source tools they form three operational segments: procedural (command pipelines), contextual (principle and template injection), and verification (merge-blocking gates).

The market structure signals one thing. Five frameworks exceed 10,000 stars, five have fewer than 1,000, and five have no public metric at all — and it’s precisely in that invisible cohort that the tools with the highest formal rigor live. If you view SDD through the lens of two or three popular candidates, MUSUBI, CSDD, and Intent disappear off the radar — yet they offer the highest rigor the ecosystem has. An architect’s first task: see all fifteen before you start filtering.

How do you rationally organize these fifteen? We need an axis — and it’s the three-level rigor taxonomy.

Three Kinds of Engineering Contract

“Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.” — Dwight D. Eisenhower, 34th President of the United States

Eisenhower says something every enterprise architect has heard hundreds of times — and that returns today in a new form. A plan as a static document is worthless. Planning as a living process is everything. This exact distinction is what Deepak Babu Piskala (arXiv:2602.00180, 2026) codified in his three-level SDD rigor taxonomy. In my consulting experience, it’s the best tool-selection heuristic the 2026 ecosystem has to offer.

Level one — Spec-First — is a preliminary contract, a letter of intent. You write the spec before the code; it lives in the feature-branch cycle, and after merging, it becomes historical documentation. The promise to the organization: flexibility. Adoption cost: low. Ten of the fifteen frameworks live here — Spec-Kit, Superpowers, BMAD, GSD, SpecSwarm, cc-sdd, Don Cheli SDD, Agent OS v3, Shotgun CLI, WordPress SDD, OWASP Skill.

Level two — Spec-Anchored — is BIM documentation with addendums. The spec lives through the entire project lifecycle; every change requires an addendum; every addendum propagates to design, code, and tests. The promise: auditability and traceability. Cost: higher process overhead, requires a team that’s mature enough process-wise. Representatives: MUSUBI (orthodoxy), Intent (modern Living Spec), OpenSpec (brownfield-first).

Level three — Spec-as-Source — is the CNC model. The spec is the only edited artifact. Code literally contains the comment // GENERATED FROM SPEC - DO NOT EDIT. The promise: a guarantee by construction, zero spec drift by design. Cost: aspirational in 2026 outside OSS libraries and security-critical contexts. Representatives: Tessl and CSDD.

Running through all three levels is one pattern — the Constitution Pattern. Six of the fifteen frameworks implement it: a constitution.md file with inviolable project principles, loaded by the agent at every session, like a company's internal rulebook. The pattern debuted in Spec-Kit in the second half of 2025; academic formalization came from S. R. Marri's work (arXiv:2602.02584, 2026) in the form of Constitutional SDD, which empirically reduces measurable security defects by 73% while preserving team velocity.

The critical interpretive trap — most developers equate “higher rigor” with “better.” That’s wrong. Higher rigor means a higher cost that pays off only when the project actually needs it. Before choosing a framework, write down in one sentence: what obligation must my spec deliver — flexibility (L1), auditability (L2), or a guarantee by construction (L3)? Without an answer to that question, all matrix comparisons are intellectual theater.

We have three levels. At each one, tools differ in what they install. Time to look at the artifacts.

What .specify/ Actually Contains

Most authors describing Spec-Kit reduce it to “nine slash commands.” That’s misleading. Spec-Kit’s real power lies in the persistent artifacts it enforces — in constitution.md as the overriding context and in three templates that enforce specification structure.

After specify init --ai claude, four persistent artifacts land in the repository along with a pipeline of nine slash commands:

.specify/memory/constitution.md
.specify/templates/spec-template.md
.specify/templates/plan-template.md
.specify/templates/tasks-template.md
.claude/commands/speckit.{constitution,specify,plan,tasks,implement}.md

constitution.md is the heart of the system. It contains nine articles, each with a MUST/SHOULD/MAY level. A code conflict with any article blocks the merge. Here is the verbatim opening of the first:

Article I — Library-First Principle: Every feature in Specify MUST begin its existence as a standalone library. No feature shall be implemented directly within application code without first being abstracted into a reusable library component.

Then follow: Article II (CLI Interface Mandate), Article III (Test-First Imperative), Article IV (Integration-First Gate), Article V (Anti-Abstraction Gate), Article VI (Simplicity Gate), Article VII (Observability Over Opacity), Article VIII (Modularity Over Monoliths), Article IX (Integration Over Isolation). Nine articles, three levels of commitment, one contract the AI agent must read before writing the first line of code.

Spec-Kit Pipeline: Enforced Order

The five-command pipeline is an enforced sequencing mechanism. The CLI programmatically prevents running /speckit.implement without an existing spec.md, plan.md, and tasks.md. Prerequisites are controlled in code, not in the prompt — the agent can't circumvent this.

The spec.md template enforces: User Stories (P0/P1/P2), Functional Requirements (FR-001..FR-NNN), Success Criteria (SC-001..SC-NNN). The plan.md template — architecture, stack, implementation phases. The tasks.md template — a list of T001..T0NN items with priority and parallelism markers.

Where Spec-Kit consciously stops: after the PR merges, the spec stays as historical documentation and isn’t actively maintained. That’s an architectural decision, not a defect — Spec-First, not Spec-Anchored. The cost of that flexibility shows up in measurable overhead too: an empirical measurement from November 2025 showed 33 minutes and 30 seconds of agent time on Spec-Kit vs. 8 minutes on a minimal baseline workflow. Adopting Spec-Kit is a deliberate acceptance of a tenfold slowdown in the first cycle in exchange for structure.

The key insight for practitioners — when you install Spec-Kit, you’re installing four artifacts, not nine commands. If your team isn’t ready to maintain constitution.md as a living document, choose a lower-overhead tool (Shotgun CLI as a generator, Agent OS as a standards layer). If it is — Spec-Kit will be your baseline for the year.

Spec-Kit is well known. The tool with the greatest adoption in 2026 is one that almost nobody analyzes — Superpowers with its 166,000 stars.

Superpowers — The Plugin with Ironclad Discipline

Superpowers is the most popular SDD framework of 2026 not because of academic rigor, but because of three concrete things: a zero-friction install, a HARD-GATE in prompts that blocks implementation without an approved design, and TDD as an iron law. Let me show you exactly what that means operationally.

Installation is literally one command:

/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official
/plugin reload

No external dependencies. No CLI. No configuration directories in the repo, aside from the optional docs/superpowers/ for designs and plans. The plugin installs a set of skill files into ~/.claude/plugins/superpowers/: brainstorming/SKILL.md, writing-plans/SKILL.md, test-driven-development/SKILL.md, using-git-worktrees/SKILL.md, subagent-driven-development/SKILL.md, executing-plans/SKILL.md. Each skill is a single Markdown file with instructions activated by keywords in the prompt.

A sub-agent — to clarify the term — is an independent AI agent spawned by the primary agent with an isolated context window. Claude Code natively supports this mechanism through the Task tool.

Wave-Based Execution: Four Waves

The Superpowers architecture is wave-based execution — a pattern for dividing work into four waves, each with a dedicated agent and a fresh context:

  • Wave 1 — Brainstorming — Socratic questions, 2–3 approaches, user approval required before proceeding
  • Wave 2 — Plan — plan generated via writing-plans/SKILL.md, detailed task breakdown
  • Wave 3 — Implementation prep — test-driven-development/SKILL.md + executing-plans/SKILL.md
  • Wave 4 — Dev Task — RED-GREEN-REFACTOR per task, commit after each task

Between Wave 1 and Wave 2 sits the HARD-GATE — a blocker defined in brainstorming/SKILL.md. No line of production code before an approved design and a failing test. This isn't a suggestion. It's a literal, blocking sentence in the prompt:

Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it.

The second iron law — the TDD iron law — is equally blunt:

NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST.

It’s enforced by Claude Code subagents checking actual test output (“14 tests pass, 0 failing”), not an agent’s declaration. After the Implementation phase, two review subagents spawn — a spec compliance reviewer and a code quality reviewer. Each gets a fresh context; each returns a PASS or FAIL verdict.

If it fails — the task isn’t marked complete. The context is reset to eliminate one of the most painful problems in AI coding — context rot, the degradation of agent response quality during long sessions as the context window fills with historical noise.

Why TDD Needs a Blocker, Not a Request

Kent Beck — the canonical author of TDD — described this problem on The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast in 2025. In a loose paraphrase from the interview: the genie doesn’t want to do TDD — it wants to write code and then add tests that pass. Superpowers doesn’t ask the agent for tests. It blocks it programmatically until it has actually written a failing test.

The criticism is familiar and fair. On HackerNews, a thread about Superpowers collected hundreds of points; one of the most-read comments read: “Maybe not highly overengineered but definitely somewhat. I ended up stripping it back to get something useful. Kept maybe 30%.” Superpowers is opinionated — not every developer wants a HARD-GATE.

The framework also consciously goes no further: no traceability (no REQ-XXX-NNN), no brownfield support (no delta specs), Claude Code only (no Cursor, Codex, Gemini). These aren’t design flaws. They’re focus.

The practical conclusion for a solo developer or small team working in Claude Code — Superpowers is the cheapest possible quality gate. Cost: one install command plus acceptance that you won’t write code without a design and a test. Return: the elimination of the three most common AI coding mistakes (missing test, skipped design, production code without review).

HARD-GATE is great discipline for a solo dev. What happens when the project grows, the team scales to ten or twenty people, and compliance starts asking about REQ→Test traceability?

MUSUBI — EARS, C4, Traceability Matrix

MUSUBI has 28 GitHub stars. It also has the highest formal rigor in the ecosystem. That paradox isn’t a market failure — it’s a signal that most SDD teams don’t need full formality. Only those that must deliver it to an auditor do.

Installation via npx musubi-sdd@latest init creates a .claude/skills/ directory with 25–31 skills activated by keywords: @orchestrator, @requirements-analyst (EARS), @system-architect (C4 + ADR), @test-engineer (TDD), @traceability-auditor (100% coverage), @constitution-enforcer (nine articles), @security-auditor (OWASP).

EARS: A Format from Rolls-Royce Aerospace

The EARS format — Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax — is a requirements-writing standard with five patterns that eliminate ambiguity. It requires SHALL or MUST and forbids should, may, could, might, would. It comes from Rolls-Royce aerospace (author — Alistair Mavin). It looks literally like this:

REQ-AUTH-001 [Ubiquitous]:
  The system SHALL hash all passwords using bcrypt with cost factor ≥ 12
REQ-AUTH-002 [Event-Driven]:
  WHEN user submits login form with valid credentials,
  the system SHALL return JWT token valid for 15 minutesREQ-AUTH-003 [Unwanted Behaviour]:
  IF login fails 5 times within 15 minutes,
  THEN the system SHALL lock the account for 30 minutes

These are three of the five patterns; the remaining two — State-Driven (WHILE ... the system SHALL ...) and Optional Feature (WHERE ... the system SHALL ...) — complete the palette. Every requirement has an identifier. Every requirement will be reflected in the traceability matrix.

Traceability Matrix and Blocking Gates

The traceability matrix is the mechanism linking a requirement to design, code, and test. In MUSUBI, it looks like this:

  • REQ-AUTH-001 → design/auth-component.md § 2 → src/auth/service.ts:45 → tests/auth.test.ts:12
  • REQ-AUTH-002 → design/auth-component.md § 3 → src/auth/jwt.ts:78 → tests/jwt.test.ts:34
  • REQ-AUTH-003 → design/auth-component.md § 4 → src/auth/throttle.ts:22 → tests/throttle.test.ts:9

The @traceability-auditor skill generates this matrix automatically and blocks the merge if coverage drops below 100%. Combined with C4 + ADR — a model of hierarchical architecture diagrams (Context / Container / Component / Code) linked with Architecture Decision Records — it gives an architect everything an enterprise auditor needs.

MUSUBI’s nine constitutional articles have three criticality levels: critical (blocking), advisory, flexible. The critical ones are Article III (Test-First), Article IV (EARS Format), Article V (100% Traceability). The @constitution-enforcer skill checks every file before merging — a violation blocks the PR.

For brownfield projects, MUSUBI has a dedicated mode — sdd-change-init plus the @change-impact-analyzer skill, which generates delta specs (a spec describing only changes — ADDED/MODIFIED/REMOVED — relative to the current state; git diff for business requirements). Workflow modes small / medium / large with varying quality thresholds allow the process to scale.

Two other L2 frameworks round out the Spec-Anchored landscape. Intent (Augment Code, $252 million in funding) — bidirectional Living Spec with agent roles of Coordinator, Specialists in isolated git worktrees, and a Verifier that atomically updates the spec when the agent discovers an API change or a missing requirement. OpenSpec (5.8k stars) — the lightest L2, built around delta specs as its core, ideal for incremental changes in a legacy codebase.

A practical decision heuristic. Write down the answer to one question: how many times in the past year did someone ask about requirements-to-test traceability? Zero times — stay on L1. Once — move to L2 (MUSUBI). More than once, or if the project has a greater than 80% chance of being audited in the next year — L2 plus CSDD as a security layer. MUSUBI pays back its investment before the auditor asks the first question. For every other team, MUSUBI’s overhead is unjustifiable.

L2 solves traceability. There’s one more approach — banning manual code editing altogether.

When Code Stops Being Written

“Perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing more to take away.” — Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, writer

Spec-as-Source is exactly that — an act of subtraction. You subtract the right to manually edit code. Only the spec remains. Code becomes a generated artifact, annotated with // GENERATED FROM SPEC - DO NOT EDIT. In 2026, this is still a horizon, not a production default — but a horizon every architect must understand.

Tessl: You Edit the Spec, Not the Code

The Tessl Framework — the work of Guy Podjarny, an industry veteran from Snyk, backed by $125 million — operates on a .spec.md file with four inline annotations: @generate, @describe, @test, @use. YAML frontmatter is optional. This is what it literally looks like:

---
title: JWT Authentication Service
version: 1.0.0
---
# JWT Auth Spec@generate src/auth/jwt-service.ts
@test src/auth/__tests__/jwt-service.test.ts## Requirements
The system SHALL validate JWT tokens on every API request. [REQ-AUTH-001]
WHEN token is expired,
the system SHALL return HTTP 401 with error message "Token expired". [REQ-AUTH-002]

After tessl build, the file src/auth/jwt-service.ts literally begins with the comment:

// GENERATED FROM SPEC - DO NOT EDIT

Then — code. Exactly the code that corresponds to the specification. To change behavior, you edit .spec.md, run tessl build, and the code regenerates. You edit the spec, not the code. That's the discipline of subtraction.

The second component of the Tessl ecosystem is the Spec Registry — a registry of verified library specifications. Podjarny described the mechanism briefly (paraphrased from Tessl sources):

Pre-populated the registry with over 10,000 usage specs, pre-generated by analyzing the code of specific versions of libraries and additional information about those libraries from usage online. — Guy Podjarny, founder of Tessl

The analogy — a package manager (like npm) for AI-ready knowledge. Instead of hallucinating a library's API, the agent installs a verified specification and operates on it.

Registry Architecture and CSDD

The registry architecture is a Split Manifest System — tessl.json (a structural version controller resolving dependency paths) plus KNOWLEDGE.md (a narrative format for LLM attention). The split eliminates the tension between machine-readable and human-readable formats.

Added to that is an Eval Framework with the --prs flag — Tessl compiles two code variants: "with context" (with the spec) and a baseline without context. If the difference is negligible, the spec is a token filler and gets dropped from the registry.

CSDD — Constitutional Spec-Driven Development by Marri — is Spec-as-Source with a security-by-construction layer. Security is built in through constraint (a rule violation REJECTS code), not through after-the-fact auditing. A verbatim constitutional clause looks like this:

## SEC-001 (CWE-89) — SQL Injection Prevention
Level: MUST
All database queries MUST use parameterized queries or ORM.
Direct string concatenation in SQL is PROHIBITED.
Enforcement: Static analysis (semgrep rule: sql-injection)
Violation: Reject implementation, require rewrite.

Each rule has a SEC-NNN identifier, a CWE Reference mapping, a MUST/SHOULD/MAY level, an implementation pattern, and a Compliance Traceability Matrix mapping the rule to lines of code. The empirical result in banking microservices — a 73% reduction in security defects compared to unconstrained AI generation, with no degradation of team velocity. That’s a number a CISO and an auditor understand without explanation.

My approach in 2026 looks like this. Spec-First for 80% of projects. Spec-Anchored for regulated ones. Spec-as-Source I’m watching, not deploying — until Tessl exits closed beta and I’ve seen a third independent enterprise case study.

The Tessl Framework is in closed beta, the Spec Registry in open beta; the registry covers 10,000 libraries. For fintech clients, I start the CSDD conversation on the first project; for e-commerce clients, I don’t enter Spec-as-Source until the end of 2027. A practitioner who doesn’t understand L3 will be asking what these tessl.json and KNOWLEDGE.md files are doing everywhere in eighteen months. Worth understanding now.

We have the full picture — fifteen frameworks, three levels, concrete artifacts. Time to turn that into a decision path.

The Matrix and Four Decision Paths

The full matrix of fifteen frameworks across eight dimensions is a reference chart. The four typical project contexts are recommendations. Together they give you a five-minute decision if you know the context — or the realization that your real problem isn’t tool selection; it’s a lack of context categorization.

The Hidden Dividing Axis: TDD as a Meta-Choice

The ecosystem’s hidden dividing axis is TDD. Mandatory in Superpowers (via the HARD-GATE in brainstorming/SKILL.md), Don Cheli SDD (programmatic gate — TypeScript orchestrator blocks the merge without coverage above 85%), and MUSUBI (Article III, blocking). Optional in Spec-Kit, BMAD, GSD, cc-sdd.

Choosing a framework with mandatory TDD is a meta-choice about whether you trust the agent or block it. Kent Beck suggests blocking is rational.

Four Decision Contexts

Context A — Solo or small team, greenfield, experiment or MVP. Choose Spec-Kit with the lean preset, optionally plus Superpowers in Claude Code for the HARD-GATE and TDD. Large community, no vendor lock-in (over 20 agents supported natively according to Spec-Kit's official documentation), minimal overhead. Startup command:

specify init projekt --ai claude
specify preset add lean

Context B — Team of over ten people, enterprise, compliance (SOC2, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF). Choose MUSUBI in large mode plus CSDD as a security layer. 100% REQ→Design→Code→Test traceability is required by auditors; EARS eliminates interpretive ambiguity; CSDD delivers a Compliance Traceability Matrix down to code-line granularity. Startup command:

npx musubi-sdd@latest init

Context C — Brownfield, legacy codebase, adding a feature to an existing product. Choose OpenSpec plus Shotgun CLI. Delta Specs (ADDED/MODIFIED/REMOVED) fit the nature of brownfield work; Shotgun indexes the repository and builds a code graph before you write the first line of the spec. Startup command:

uvx shotgun plan "Add OAuth2"
openspec propose add-oauth2

Context D — Security-critical (fintech, healthcare, embedded automotive). Choose CSDD plus MUSUBI plus the OWASP Security Skill. A 73% reduction in security defects is the number for a CISO; the Compliance Traceability Matrix is required by regulators; CWE/MITRE Top 25 as a constitutional baseline. Workflow: MUSUBI init → constitution based on CWE references → OWASP Skill in .claude/skills/ → audit via @security-auditor.

Meta-Decision: Context Before Framework

The meta-decision I see most often in consulting — before you choose a framework, write your context in one sentence. If you can’t, the problem is in front of you, not in the ecosystem.

Most dysfunctional SDD deployments I’ve seen at clients began with “I want to choose the best tool” rather than “I want to solve a specific problem X for team Y in context Z.” The next time someone asks “which SDD framework,” answer with context, not a list of tools.

Four recommendations for today. Where is the entire ecosystem headed on the 2026+ horizon?

The Horizon — MCP, AGENTS.md, Living Spec

Three emerging trends indicate that in eighteen months, the choice of an SDD framework will look entirely different. Investing in spec engineering in 2026 is investing in a competency that will be rare in a year.

MCP: USB-C for Agents

MCP (Model Context Protocol) — Anthropic’s standardized protocol (November 2024) for integrating tools and context with AI agents. Analogy: USB-C for agents. Transferred to the Linux Foundation (December 2025), currently 97 million monthly SDK downloads (April 2026).

The official two-layer architecture — the transport layer (stdio, HTTP) and the protocol layer (JSON-RPC) — replaces the fragmentation of Markdown / TOML / YAML formats. Every SDD framework with an MCP server gets instant integration with all MCP-aware agents. Tessl already uses MCP as its universal agent protocol.

AGENTS.md: package.json for Agent Behavior

AGENTS.md — a file in the repo’s root directory describing rules and a contract for AI agents; OpenAI, Google, and others treat it as a cross-tool standard. Currently over 60,000 OSS projects; co-creators: OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules (Google), Cursor, Factory; stewardship under the Linux Foundation. Analogy — package.json, but for agent behavior. One file, and many tools know what to do. OpenAI Codex supports it natively; Cursor supports AGENTS.md in current versions.

Living Spec as Infrastructure

Living Spec as infrastructure — Intent is the pioneer: a spec actively synchronized with code, agent-writable, with a Verifier as a regulator. The direction of evolution is clear: the spec stops being a document and becomes a database of intent — just as package.json is infrastructure for a package manager. In eighteen months, this will be the default, not the exception.

In parallel, vibe-coding as a separate category is disappearing. It’s becoming an antipattern like goto in the 1970s. Spec-Kit had 72,000–77,000 stars in March 2026 and grew to ~90,000 by April 2026 — that's an adoption rate, not a static number. Whoever writes production code through bare LLMs without specifications in 2026 will be in the position of a developer who didn't adopt version control in 2005.

What’s worth watching in the coming quarters? Will the Tessl Spec Registry catch up to npm in library coverage? Will enterprises get a ready-made Audit Trail SaaS (BMAD and Qodo are already signaling this)? Will AGENTS.md be formalized by a standards body (W3C, IETF)? Will Kiro IDE from AWS normalize approval gates as an enterprise standard?

My practical recommendation — add “spec engineering competency” to your 2026 roadmap, even if you’re not deploying SDD this year. People who can do this will be rare in eighteen months. The best next step: pick one low-risk project and run Spec-Kit with the lean preset on it for two weeks. Write down what works, what doesn't. That's your baseline.

Summary

Returning to the opening. 166,000 vs. 28 isn’t a paradox. It’s the market structure — and at the same time the best SDD tool-selection heuristic there is, if you know how to read it.

Fifteen SDD frameworks aren’t fifteen competitors — they’re market segments matched to different contexts. You don’t choose the “best” one; you choose the “right” one.

Three rigor levels (Piskala 2026) are the compass — not GitHub star counts. Spec-First for 80% of projects, Spec-Anchored for regulated ones, Spec-as-Source you watch, you don’t deploy.

Artifacts tell you more than stars. Spec-Kit installs .specify/ with nine constitutional articles. Superpowers — a plugin with a HARD-GATE in brainstorming/SKILL.md and the TDD iron law. MUSUBI — 25+ skills with EARS and a traceability matrix. Tessl — .spec.md with // GENERATED FROM SPEC. You choose the tool — you choose the artifacts you'll have to maintain.

Four contexts, four recommendations. Spec-Kit with the lean preset for solo greenfield. MUSUBI plus CSDD for enterprise compliance. OpenSpec plus Shotgun for brownfield. CSDD plus MUSUBI plus OWASP Skill for security-critical.

Horizon 2026+ — MCP, AGENTS.md, Living Spec. Start building spec engineering competency today.
